overview.summary: Learn to turn raw business data into decisions with spreadsheets, SQL, Python, dashboards and AI assistants, and to check what the AI produces. Ten practical modules set in Indian businesses, a final assessment, and a portfolio project with a mentor.
overview.audience: students and graduates who want an entry-level data analyst role, or to use data well in any job
outcomes: Turn a vague business question into an analysis plan with a clear decision
Clean, combine and summarise data in Excel, SQL and Python (pandas)
Tell a real change from noise using samples, spread and simple experiments
Build a dashboard that tracks what matters and flags problems early
Use AI assistants to work faster, and verify everything they produce
Present a recommendation a manager can act on, backed by a portfolio project

items.statement: Before I answer a question with numbers, I check exactly what is being asked.
I notice when a statistic in the news or on social media doesn’t add up.
I take the numbers in reports at face value.
I use formulas instead of working things out by hand.
I sort or filter a spreadsheet to find the rows I need, instead of scrolling through it.
Spreadsheets with more than a few hundred rows overwhelm me.
I spot typos, duplicates and inconsistent entries in lists.
I keep a copy of the original file before I change any data.
I start working with data without checking it first.
When I need one number from a long list, I write down the steps (which rows, which groups, which total) before I start.
I look up the exact syntax of a formula or command instead of guessing it.
When I need figures from a large table, I ask someone else to pull them for me.
I ask how many people a survey asked before I trust its result.
When I see an average, I look at the highest and lowest values behind it.
When two things happen together, I assume one causes the other.
When I repeat the same steps on a file every week, I look for a way to automate them.
When a tool shows an error, I read it and try to fix it myself.
I avoid tasks that involve typing commands or code.
I choose charts that make the main point obvious.
I notice when a chart’s design exaggerates a difference.
I add as many charts as I can to show I’ve been thorough.
I use AI tools to speed up my studies or work.
I check an AI tool’s answer against another source before relying on it.
If an AI tool sounds confident, I trust its answer.
When I share a finding, I explain what it means in two or three sentences.
I start a presentation with my main point.

modules.title: Thinking like an analyst
modules.summary: Turn vague questions into answerable ones, know your data types, and read averages critically.
modules.outcome: Turn a vague business question into one you can answer with data, and pick numbers that answer it fairly: the right type, the right average and a fair comparison.

learn.title: Start with the decision, not the data
learn.body:
An analysis is only useful if it changes a decision. Before you open a spreadsheet, write down who will decide, what they will decide, and what would change their mind. “How are sales doing?” becomes “Should we keep the Diwali discount running in Pune next week?”: a question with an owner, a deadline and an action.

Then pin down every vague word. If a founder says the app “feels quieter”, that could mean fewer sign-ups, fewer orders or shorter visits, and each one needs different data. Agree on the measure and the period before you start. If the request already names the decision, the measure and the period, it is ready: start the analysis instead of asking again. A common beginner mistake is to pull every number available and hope an answer appears: you end up with a long report and no decision.

learn.title: Know your data types
learn.body:
Some numbers can be added: revenue in ₹, minutes, quantities. Some only look like numbers: PIN codes, phone numbers and order IDs are labels, so their average means nothing, and a spreadsheet may even drop a leading zero (the code 00125 becomes 125). Then there are categories (city, payment method), dates and free text.

Many early mistakes come from treating one type as another: averaging PIN codes, adding up order IDs, or sorting dates stored as text, so that “10/01/2026” comes before “9/01/2026”. A quick test: would adding two values together give a meaningful number? If not, the column is a label or a category. Count it or group by it instead of summing it.

learn.title: Averages hide, and together isn’t cause
learn.body:
An average order value of ₹850 can mean every order is about ₹850, or that most orders are ₹300 and a few bulk orders are ₹20,000. Before trusting one number, check the spread: the minimum, the maximum and the median (the middle value once you sort them). When a few huge values pull the mean far above the median, the median describes a typical customer better. The mean is still the right figure when you need a total: 200 orders × a ₹850 mean is ₹1.7 lakh of sales.

Be just as careful when two numbers move together: that doesn’t mean one causes the other. Customers with a café’s loyalty card spend more per visit, but the card may not be why: regular big spenders are the most likely to sign up. When people choose something themselves (self-selection), they often differ in other ways too. Only a fair comparison, such as a randomly assigned test (module 6), shows cause.

tasks.title: Sharpen a vague question
tasks.prompt: A café chain’s owner asks: “Why are we losing customers?” Rewrite this as two or three specific questions you could answer with data. For each, say what data you would need and what decision it would inform.
tasks.hint: Name the time period, which customers you mean, and what “losing” looks like in the data (for example, no visit in 60 days).

tasks.title: Spot the wrong type
tasks.prompt: List five columns you would expect in an online store’s orders file. For each, give its data type and one mistake someone could make if they treated it as a different type.
tasks.hint: An order ID looks like a number. Would you ever add order IDs together?

reflection.prompt: Think of a decision you made recently: a phone, a course, a trip. What data did you use, and what data do you wish you had?
reflection.hint: Small personal decisions use the same habits as business ones.

quiz.title: The report by Friday
quiz.scenario: The founder of Saffron Basket, an online grocer, writes: “Customers keep saying deliveries take ages. On Friday I’ll decide which cities get extra riders, so show me every city that delivered fewer than 90% of its orders within our 30-minute promise over the last four weeks.” You have 18 months of orders (date, city, basket value, delivery minutes, customer ID) and two days.
quiz.question: What is the best first step?
options: Work out each city’s share of orders delivered within 30 minutes over the last four weeks
Ask the founder what she will decide with the report, and agree which measure of delay she means
Compare this week’s order count with last week’s, city by city, to find where orders dropped
Chart orders, basket value and delivery times for all 18 months, so the founder sees every angle
quiz.explanation: The founder has already given the decision (where extra riders go), the measure (the share of orders within 30 minutes, against 90%), the breakdown (each city) and the period (the last four weeks). The question is ready to answer, so the first step is to work out that share for each city.
quiz.why_wrong: Asking what she will decide and which measure she means is the right first step when a request is vague, such as “orders feel slower”, but she has already named the decision, the measure and the period, so it spends one of your two days on questions she has answered; order counts would be right if she had said orders were falling, but her question is about delivery times; charting everything suits an open brief with no deadline, and here it buries the one answer she asked for.
quiz.learning_outcome: Once a request names the decision, the measure and the period, answer it; ask questions when it doesn’t.

quiz.title: The intern’s summary sheet
quiz.scenario: An intern at a delivery app has added a row of averages under every column of the customer orders table.
quiz.question: Which of these averages is meaningless?
options: Average customer PIN code: 411,027
Average items per order: 3.4
Average delivery time: 31 minutes
Average customer rating: 4.3 out of 5
quiz.explanation: A PIN code is a label written in digits. Adding two PIN codes gives no meaningful number, so neither does their average.
quiz.why_wrong: 3.4 items is a real average even though no single order has 0.4 of an item; delivery minutes are a quantity, so their average means something, even if a few slow orders pull it up; star ratings are averaged all the time, and 4.3 tells you how customers rate the service on the whole.
quiz.learning_outcome: Check a column’s type before you summarise it: labels are counted, not averaged.

quiz.title: Fees at a study centre
quiz.scenario: A study centre has 50 students. 47 pay a monthly fee of between ₹2,000 and ₹2,500, and three corporate-sponsored students pay ₹30,000 each. The sponsorships continue next term.
quiz.question: The owner wants one fee figure to multiply by 50 to estimate next term’s monthly fee income. Which should she use?
options: The median fee, since the median isn’t pulled up by the three large fees
The median of the 47 regular fees, treating the three sponsored places as one-offs
The midpoint of the lowest and highest fees, so both ends of the range count
The mean fee, since it counts every fee in full, the three large ones too
quiz.explanation: The mean × 50 is exactly the sum of all 50 fees, ₹1.84 to ₹2.08 lakh a month, and the sponsored places continue, so their ₹90,000 belongs in the estimate. A total needs the mean, even when a few large values pull it above the typical fee.
quiz.why_wrong: The median is the right figure for what a typical student pays, such as on a fees poster, but the median × 50 gives only ₹1.0 to ₹1.25 lakh, leaving out most of the ₹90,000 the sponsored places bring; leaving the sponsored fees out would be right if those places were ending, but they continue; the midpoint, ₹16,000, is set by the two extremes and, × 50, gives ₹8 lakh, which no one will pay.
quiz.learning_outcome: Use the mean when you need a total, and the median when you need the typical case.

quiz.title: Dark mode and test scores
quiz.scenario: Last month a coaching app switched dark mode on for a randomly chosen half of its 40,000 new users; the other half kept the light theme. The dark-mode half scored 12% higher in the app’s tests, a gap far larger than chance would make with 20,000 users in each half. The product manager wants to make dark mode the default to raise scores.
quiz.question: What is the soundest response?
options: Not yet: dark-mode users may be keener students, so test it on random users first
Not yet: first survey students on whether they actually prefer dark mode or not
Partly: turn it on only for evening sessions, when dark screens are easiest to read
Agree: the app chose at random who got dark mode, so the gap comes from the setting
quiz.explanation: The app, not the students, decided who got dark mode, and it did so at random, so keen and casual students are spread across both halves. That makes it a fair comparison, and a clear gap can be credited to the setting.
quiz.why_wrong: Testing on random users first would be right if students had switched dark mode on themselves, but this already was a random test, so asking for another only delays the change; a survey of preferences would matter if the goal were satisfaction, but the goal is scores, and the test measured them; limiting it to evening sessions would be right if the gap appeared only in the evening, but the test compared whole months, so nothing points to evenings.
quiz.learning_outcome: When the groups were assigned at random, a clear gap shows cause, and you can act on it.

modules.title: Spreadsheets that answer questions
modules.summary: Tables, XLOOKUP and PivotTables: answer business questions in Excel or Google Sheets.
modules.outcome: Use tables, lookups and PivotTables to answer a business question in a spreadsheet.

learn.title: Make it a table first
learn.body:
Format your data as a table (Ctrl+T in Excel). Google Sheets, which is free, has tables too (Convert to table). A table needs one header row, one row per record, no blank rows and no merged cells. It doesn’t tidy these up for you, so fix them first.

Once it is a table, it grows with new data. Paste in 200 rows of next week’s orders. Every formula, filter and PivotTable built on it picks them up (a PivotTable after you click Refresh). You can also refer to columns by name, like Orders[Value]. That is easier to read than C2:C5000 and doesn’t break when the data grows.

A table changes how Excel treats the range, not what is in your cells. A number stored as text stays text, and a misspelt city stays misspelt, until you clean it.

learn.title: Lookups, and references that stay put
learn.body:
XLOOKUP finds a value in one column and returns the matching value from another, such as a product’s category from its SKU (stock-keeping unit: the shop’s code for a product):

=XLOOKUP(A2, Products[SKU], Products[Category], "Not found")

Unlike VLOOKUP, it can look left, matches exactly by default (no sorting needed), and its fourth argument says what to show when nothing is found. If it says “Not found” for a code you can see in the list, look for a hidden space, or a number stored as text: they look the same but don’t match.

When you fill a formula down, its references move: B2 becomes B3, B4 and so on. Put $ signs in a reference that must stay put: =B2*$F$1 keeps using the GST rate in F1 on every row. Press F4 to add them. On a phone, type the $ signs yourself. $F1 locks only the column, and F$1 only the row.

learn.title: Summarise with a PivotTable
learn.body:
A PivotTable groups and totals thousands of rows in seconds: revenue by city by month, or orders by payment method. Drag fields into Rows, Columns and Values, then switch Values between Sum, Count and Average as the question needs. Excel and Google Sheets both have them, so this works free.

Be careful with rates. A return rate is returned orders divided by all orders, for each group, so it needs two numbers. If 2 of 8 Pune orders came back, Pune’s return rate is 25%. “Show Values As % of Column Total” answers a different question: each payment method’s share of all returns, which makes the busiest method look worst even if its rate is low. A useful trick: if a column holds 1 for yes and 0 for no, its average is the share of yeses. The average of 1s and 0s is the share of 1s.

tasks.title: Build a return-rate PivotTable
tasks.prompt:
Copy these 12 orders from an online saree store into Google Sheets (free, in a browser or the Sheets app) or Excel, with three columns, order_id, payment and returned (1 = returned, 0 = kept):
1001,UPI,0
1002,COD,1
1003,UPI,0
1004,Card,0
1005,COD,1
1006,COD,0
1007,UPI,1
1008,Card,0
1009,COD,1
1010,UPI,0
1011,COD,0
1012,Card,1
Build a PivotTable with payment in Rows and the average of returned in Values. Write down each method’s return rate, then check one rate by hand (returned orders ÷ all orders). (About 35 minutes.)
tasks.hint: Count COD’s rows yourself: how many of them were returned? Check: COD returned 3 of 5 orders (60%), Card 1 of 3 (33%), UPI 1 of 4 (25%). If your PivotTable shows other numbers, look at whether Values is set to Average, not Sum.

tasks.title: Write the lookup
tasks.prompt: On a second tab, make a price list (SKU, product, category): SR-101, Banarasi silk, Silk; SR-102, Kanjivaram, Silk; SR-205, Chanderi, Cotton; SR-310, Bandhani, Georgette. On the orders tab, add an SKU column for the first four orders: SR-101, SR-205, SR-999, and “SR-102 ” typed with a space at the end. Write an XLOOKUP that brings in the category and shows “Not found” when nothing matches. Which rows say “Not found”, and which of them is not really missing? (About 35 minutes.)
tasks.hint: Look at XLOOKUP’s fourth argument. Check: SR-101 gives Silk and SR-205 gives Cotton. SR-999 and “SR-102 ” both say “Not found”, but only SR-999 is really missing: SR-102 is in the list, and the hidden trailing space stops the match (TRIM fixes it).

reflection.prompt: What is one spreadsheet task you do, or have seen done, by hand that a table, a lookup or a PivotTable could do in seconds?
reflection.hint: Copying totals from one sheet to another counts.

quiz.title: Every Monday’s new orders
quiz.scenario: A textile wholesaler in Surat adds about 300 order rows to the same sheet every Monday, and then re-selects the ranges of every formula and PivotTable by hand.
quiz.question: What does formatting the data as an Excel Table (Ctrl+T) fix for them?
options: It removes blank rows and merged cells, so the data is clean before you analyse it
It lets you sort and filter the rows, which a plain range of cells can’t do
It sets each column’s data type, so numbers typed as text become real numbers
Formulas and PivotTables take in each week’s new rows, so ranges needn’t be redone
quiz.explanation: A table grows with new rows, so formulas and PivotTables built on it include them (a PivotTable after Refresh), and columns can be referred to by name.
quiz.why_wrong: A table doesn’t remove blank rows or merged cells: you fix those before you create it; a plain range can already be sorted and filtered; a number stored as text stays text inside a table until you convert it.
quiz.learning_outcome: Use an Excel Table so analysis keeps up as the data grows.

quiz.title: Invoices and a product master
quiz.scenario: A distributor in Indore is matching 4,000 invoice lines to a 900-row product master. Some SKUs on the invoices are new and not yet in the master.
quiz.question: Which formula returns the product category, and shows “New SKU” when there is no match?
options: =XLOOKUP(Master[SKU], B2, Master[Category], "New SKU")
=XLOOKUP(B2, Master[SKU], Master[Category], 0, "New SKU")
=IFERROR(VLOOKUP(B2, Master, 2), "New SKU")
=XLOOKUP(B2, Master[SKU], Master[Category], "New SKU")
quiz.explanation: XLOOKUP takes the value to find (B2), where to find it (Master[SKU]), what to return (Master[Category]) and what to show if nothing matches. Its default is an exact match, so a new SKU shows “New SKU”.
quiz.why_wrong: The XLOOKUP with B2 and Master[SKU] swapped looks for the whole SKU column inside one cell; the version with 0 puts 0 in the not-found slot and “New SKU” where the match mode goes, which takes a number, not text; VLOOKUP with its last argument left out does an approximate match, so a new SKU can quietly get a neighbouring SKU’s category instead of an error.
quiz.learning_outcome: Use an exact-match lookup with a clear “not found” value, and know each argument’s place.

quiz.title: Return rate by payment method
quiz.scenario: Your orders sheet has a Returned column with 1 for a returned order and 0 for a kept one. Payment method is in the Rows of your PivotTable.
quiz.question: Which Values setting shows the return rate for each payment method directly?
options: Sum of Returned, shown as % of Column Total
Count of Returned
Average of Returned
Sum of Returned
quiz.explanation: The average of a column of 1s and 0s is the share of 1s: the return rate.
quiz.why_wrong: Sum shown as % of Column Total gives each method’s share of all returns, which makes the busiest method look worst; Count of Returned counts every order, returned or not; Sum of Returned is the number of returns, not a rate, so a busy method looks worse even with a low rate.
quiz.learning_outcome: Averaging a 1/0 column gives a rate.

quiz.title: GST on every row
quiz.scenario: Cell F1 holds the GST rate. In C2 you write =B2*$F$1 and fill it down to C500.
quiz.question: What do the dollar signs in $F$1 do as you fill down?
options: Keep the column on F but let the row move, so C3 uses F2 and C4 uses F3
Fix the row on 1 only, so F1 stays put going down but shifts if copied across
Keep pointing at F1 on every row, while B2 moves to B3, B4 and so on
Store F1’s current rate in each row, so a later change to F1 doesn’t alter them
quiz.explanation: $F$1 is an absolute reference: both the column and the row stay fixed wherever the formula is copied, so every row uses the GST rate in F1, while the relative B2 moves down.
quiz.why_wrong: A column-only lock is $F1, which would move to F2, F3 down the rows; a row-only lock is F$1, which would shift if copied across, while $F$1 stays put in both directions; the formula still reads F1 live, so changing the rate in F1 updates every row.
quiz.learning_outcome: Use $ to fix a reference every row must share, and know which part each $ fixes.

modules.title: Cleaning messy data
modules.summary: Profile data, fix duplicates, dates and inconsistent categories, and handle blanks honestly.
modules.outcome: Find and fix the problems that make analysis wrong, and keep a record of each fix.

learn.title: Profile before you clean
learn.body:
Before you change anything, count the rows, then check every column: how many blanks, how many unique values, the minimum and the maximum. Profiling shows what is broken: “Bengaluru”, “Bangalore”, “bangalore ” and “BLR” in one city column, ages of 0 and 212, fees stored as the text “₹500” beside the number 500, and dates in two formats.

Dates need special care. 03/04/2026 could be 3 April or 4 March. Look for a value whose first part is above 12, such as 13/05/2026: it can only be day/month/year. Check a few dates against something you know, such as an order you remember. Write down what you found before you fix anything, so you can show the counts before and after.

learn.title: Fix the cause, and keep a record
learn.body:
Standardise categories with a mapping table (every variant in one column, the name you want in the next), trim spaces and fix capitals, convert text into proper dates and numbers, and remove true duplicates. A true duplicate is the same record twice: the same order ID with identical values in every column. Two rows with the same name or phone number may be two real people, such as siblings who share a family phone, so don’t remove rows on one column alone. And never delete rows just to make your count match another team’s total.

Never clean silently. Keep the raw file untouched, and write each step in a cleaning log: what you changed, why, and how many rows it affected, so anyone can repeat it. Power Query in Excel, or a Python script, makes the steps repeatable. After mapping, check that nothing is left unmapped.

learn.title: Missing is not zero
learn.body:
A blank delivery time is unknown, not 0 minutes. Filling it with 0 makes deliveries look faster; filling it with the average hides how many were missing. Decide column by column: leave it blank and exclude it from that calculation, fill it from another source, or flag it. Say how many rows each choice affects.

Then ask the most important question: are the missing rows different from the rest? Suppose a clinic’s waiting times are blank mostly for patients who gave up and left. Leaving those rows out removes the longest waits, so the average looks better than what patients lived through. If the blanks are a random mix, excluding them changes little. Either way, report the share that is missing beside the result: “Average wait 22 minutes, from the 91% of visits with a recorded time.”

tasks.title: Clean a clinic export
tasks.prompt:
Copy these rows into Google Sheets or Excel, as patient_id, date, department, fee:
P01,03/04/2026,Cardio,₹500
P02,2026-04-03,cardiology,500
P03,13/04/2026,CARDIOLOGY ,500
P04,14/04/2026,Ortho,₹700
P04,14/04/2026,Ortho,₹700
P05,2026-04-15,orthopaedics,700
P06,16/04/2026,Ortho,
P07,17/04/2026,Cardio,₹500
Keep this raw tab untouched. On a new tab, make one date format, two department names, and fees as numbers. Remove only true duplicates and decide what to do with the blank fee. Write a cleaning log (step, why, rows affected), and give the row count before and after. (About 35 minutes.)
tasks.hint: Which date tells you whether 03/04/2026 is day-first? Are both P04 rows the same in every column? Check: 8 rows become 7 (only the second P04 row goes). You end with two department names, all dates in one format, and P06’s blank fee left blank and flagged, not changed to 0.

tasks.title: Decide about blanks
tasks.prompt: In a delivery dataset of 5,000 rows, 6% of rows (300) have no delivery time, and the average of the rest is 31 minutes. Give two ways to handle the blanks, and explain how each choice could change the average delivery time you report. (About 20 minutes.)
tasks.hint: Who is likely to be missing: fast deliveries, slow ones, or a random mix? Check: filling the 300 blanks with 0 pulls the average down to about 29 minutes (31 × 0.94), which looks faster than the truth. Leaving them out keeps 31, from 4,700 rows, and you say so.

reflection.prompt: What is the messiest data you have seen: a form, a contact list, an attendance register? What would you fix first, and why?
reflection.hint: Think about which problem would cause the biggest wrong answer.

quiz.title: Bookings and payments
quiz.scenario: An event-ticketing startup’s bookings export has 5,200 rows, but the payments team counts 5,000 payments. 200 booking IDs appear twice. In 150 of those pairs every column matches. In the other 50, the seat number and the payment reference differ.
quiz.question: What is the right action?
options: Remove the 150 exact copies, keep only the later row of the other 50 pairs, and log both
Remove the 150 exact copies, check the other 50 against payments first, and log both
Remove the second row of all 200 pairs, since a booking ID should be unique, and log it
Keep the first 5,000 rows by booking time, so the total matches payments, and log it
quiz.explanation: The 150 pairs that match in every column are true duplicates, so keep one of each. The other 50 have different payment references, so they may be two paid bookings or a failed payment and a retry; only the payments data can tell, so check them before removing anything, and log both steps.
quiz.why_wrong: Keeping the later row would be right if the pairs shared one payment reference, so that each was a seat change saved as a new row, but different references mean two payments may have been made; removing all 200 second rows would be right if all 200 pairs were identical, but 50 differ, so real bookings could go; keeping the first 5,000 by time makes the count match by cutting the latest bookings, while copies stay in.
quiz.learning_outcome: Remove only rows that match in every column; check near-duplicates against another source first.

quiz.title: Whose date format?
quiz.scenario: A clinic’s appointment export from a new booking app has dates such as 04/05/2026, 13/05/2026 and 28/02/2026.
quiz.question: What format are the dates in?
options: Month/day/year
Year/month/day
Day/month/year
It can’t be worked out
quiz.explanation: Values like 13 and 28 in the first position can’t be months, so the first number is the day.
quiz.why_wrong: Month/day/year would have no first number above 12; year/month/day would start with the year; the large first values settle it.
quiz.learning_outcome: Use impossible values to work out an ambiguous date format.

quiz.title: Four spellings of one city
quiz.scenario: A monthly export of 40,000 leads has a city column containing “Bengaluru”, “Bangalore”, “bangalore ” and “BLR”. The same file arrives every month.
quiz.question: What is the most reliable fix?
options: Apply TRIM and PROPER to the column, so every variant becomes one consistent spelling
Use Power Query’s fuzzy matching to merge similar spellings, then count unique cities
Find and Replace each variant in turn, most common first, then count unique cities
Trim spaces, map each variant to one name in a mapping table, then list anything unmapped
quiz.explanation: A mapping table handles every variant, including ones like “BLR” that look nothing alike, and can be reused next month. Listing what is unmapped catches any new variant.
quiz.why_wrong: TRIM and PROPER fix spaces and capitals, but “Bangalore” and “Blr” stay different names; fuzzy matching won’t link “BLR” to “Bengaluru”, and it can merge different towns with similar names; Find and Replace works once, but has to be redone by hand every month and can miss “bangalore ” with its trailing space.
quiz.learning_outcome: Standardise categories with a reusable mapping, then check nothing is left.

quiz.title: The missing delivery times
quiz.scenario: In a food-delivery dataset, 8% of orders have no delivery time. Most of them are orders the customer cancelled after a long wait.
quiz.question: If you drop those rows, how does the average delivery time you report compare with what customers actually experienced?
options: It matches, because orders with no delivery time would be left out of the average anyway
It looks better than reality, because the slowest cases are the ones left out
It looks worse than reality, because the cancelled orders were the slowest ones
It can’t be judged until all 8% are traced, so hold the figure back until then
quiz.explanation: The missing rows aren’t random: they are mostly the longest waits. Leaving them out, whether by dropping them or by letting the average skip them, makes delivery look faster than customers found it.
quiz.why_wrong: It’s true the average would skip those blanks anyway, but either way it leaves out the customers who waited longest; leaving out the slowest cases makes the average shorter, not longer; the figure can be reported now, if you say what it leaves out and give the cancellations beside it.
quiz.learning_outcome: Ask why data is missing before you drop it, and which way it moves the result.

modules.title: SQL foundations: asking a database questions
modules.summary: SELECT, WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING: filter, group and summarise data in a database.
modules.outcome: Write SELECT queries that filter, sort, group and summarise data.

learn.title: One question, one query
learn.body:
SQL reads almost like a sentence: SELECT the columns, FROM a table, WHERE rows match a condition, ORDER BY a column.

SELECT city, order_value
FROM orders
WHERE order_date >= '2026-04-01'
  AND order_date < '2026-05-01'
ORDER BY order_value DESC;

This lists April’s orders, largest first. AND needs both conditions to be true; OR keeps a row if either is. Text and dates go in single quotes ('Pune'); numbers don’t.

Notice the date range: from 1 April, and before 1 May. If order_date also holds a time, BETWEEN '2026-04-01' AND '2026-04-30' misses orders placed later in the day on 30 April. You can practise free with SQLite or PostgreSQL on your own computer, or in an online SQL playground.

learn.title: GROUP BY turns rows into answers
learn.body:
COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX summarise rows, and GROUP BY decides the groups.

SELECT city, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(order_value) AS revenue
FROM orders
GROUP BY city;

This gives one row per city. Every column in SELECT is either in the GROUP BY or inside a summary function.

Watch for NULL, which means unknown: no value was recorded. COUNT(*) counts every row. COUNT(phone), SUM and AVG use only the rows where that column isn’t NULL. So if 300 of a clinic’s 2,000 patients have no recorded age, AVG(age) is the average of the 1,700 with an age, not of all 2,000, and your report should say so. Arithmetic with NULL gives NULL too: 500 − NULL is NULL. SUM over no rows at all gives NULL, not 0; COALESCE(SUM(amount), 0) turns it into 0.

learn.title: WHERE filters rows, HAVING filters groups
learn.body:
WHERE works before grouping (only paid orders); HAVING works after (only cities with more than 500 orders).

SELECT city, COUNT(*) AS orders
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'paid'
GROUP BY city
HAVING COUNT(*) > 500;

A query runs in this order: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY. That explains most “why won’t this work?” moments: WHERE can’t use COUNT or SUM, because the groups don’t exist yet when it runs.

To find missing values, write WHERE phone IS NULL, never WHERE phone = NULL. Comparing anything with NULL gives “unknown”, not true, so “= NULL” matches no rows at all, and SQL shows no error to warn you. Use IS NOT NULL for the rows that do have a value.

tasks.title: Write and run the query
tasks.hint: Filter the dates in WHERE, then GROUP BY method. Payment 3 was at 9 pm on 30 April. Is it in your result? Check: Card 1 payment, 2300; Wallet 1 payment, 800; UPI 2 payments, 570 (payments 5 and 6 fall outside April).

tasks.title: Explain a query in plain words
tasks.prompt:
Explain what this query returns, as you would to a manager who doesn’t know SQL:
SELECT city, AVG(delivery_minutes) AS avg_minutes FROM deliveries WHERE status = 'delivered' GROUP BY city HAVING COUNT(*) >= 50 ORDER BY avg_minutes; Then create a deliveries table of your own with six rows (city, status, delivery_minutes), change 50 to 2 in the query, run it, and check that the result matches what you said. (About 35 minutes.)
tasks.hint: Why might the HAVING line be there? Check: it shows each city’s average delivery time for delivered orders only, fastest city first, and leaves out cities with fewer than 50 delivered orders, whose averages are too shaky to trust. On your six rows with 2, a city with a single delivered order should be missing from the result.

reflection.prompt: Which questions at a business you know could be answered with a single GROUP BY query? Write two.
reflection.hint: Think “for each …, how many / how much …?”

quiz.title: Orders per city
quiz.scenario: A quick-commerce app’s table orders(order_id, city, order_value, order_date) has one row per order.
quiz.question: Which query gives the number of orders in each city?
options: SELECT city, COUNT(DISTINCT city) FROM orders GROUP BY city;
SELECT city, COUNT(*) FROM orders GROUP BY city;
SELECT city, COUNT(*) FROM orders ORDER BY city;
SELECT city, COUNT(*) FROM orders GROUP BY order_id;
quiz.explanation: GROUP BY city makes one group per city, and COUNT(*) counts the rows, which are orders, in each.
quiz.why_wrong: COUNT(DISTINCT city) within each city’s group is always 1; without GROUP BY, COUNT(*) counts the whole table, so most databases reject the query and SQLite returns one row; grouping by order_id makes one group per order, so every count is 1.
quiz.learning_outcome: GROUP BY the thing you say “for each” about, then count or sum within it.

quiz.title: Cities above ₹10 lakh
quiz.scenario: A furniture D2C brand’s table orders(order_id, city, order_value) has one row per order. You want the cities whose total revenue is above ₹10 lakh.
quiz.question: Which query returns them?
options: SELECT city, SUM(order_value) FROM orders WHERE SUM(order_value) > 1000000 GROUP BY city;
SELECT city, SUM(order_value) FROM orders GROUP BY city HAVING SUM(order_value) > 1000000;
SELECT city, SUM(order_value) FROM orders WHERE order_value > 1000000 GROUP BY city;
SELECT city, SUM(order_value) FROM orders GROUP BY city HAVING MAX(order_value) > 1000000;
quiz.explanation: A city’s total exists only after grouping, so the condition on it goes in HAVING, which runs after GROUP BY.
quiz.why_wrong: WHERE runs before the groups exist, so SUM can’t be used there and the query fails; WHERE order_value > 1000000 keeps only single orders above ₹10 lakh before totalling; HAVING MAX tests each city’s largest order, not its total.
quiz.learning_outcome: Filter rows with WHERE and groups with HAVING.

quiz.title: Leads without a phone number
quiz.scenario: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM leads WHERE phone = NULL; returns 0, though many leads have no phone number.
quiz.question: Why does it return 0?
options: COUNT(*) skips rows where any column is NULL, so it should be COUNT(phone) instead
Comparing with NULL gives “unknown”, so no row passes; it needs WHERE phone IS NULL
NULL needs quotes like any other text value, as in WHERE phone = 'NULL'
Missing values are tested after grouping, so the condition belongs in HAVING
quiz.explanation: NULL means unknown, so “phone = NULL” is never true and no row is counted, with no error to warn you. IS NULL is the test for a missing value.
quiz.why_wrong: COUNT(*) counts every row whatever its values, and COUNT(phone) skips exactly the blank phones you want; 'NULL' in quotes is the four-letter text NULL, which no lead has; HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY, and moving the same “= NULL” there still matches nothing.
quiz.learning_outcome: Test for missing values with IS NULL, never “= NULL”.

quiz.title: Ratings with gaps
quiz.scenario: A table ratings(order_id, stars) has 1,000 orders. 400 have no rating (NULL). AVG(stars) returns 4.2.
quiz.question: What does 4.2 describe?
options: The average of all 1,000 orders, because AVG divides by the full row count
Nothing usable: AVG returns NULL when any value in the column is NULL
The average of the 600 rated orders only; the 400 unrated ones are left out
The likely average of all 1,000 orders, since 600 ratings is a large sample
quiz.explanation: AVG, like SUM and COUNT(stars), skips NULLs (only COUNT(*) counts every row), so 4.2 is the average among the 600 rated orders. A report should say so: “4.2 stars among the 60% of orders that were rated.”
quiz.why_wrong: AVG divides by the number of non-NULL values, 600, not by all 1,000 rows; NULL arithmetic (4 + NULL is NULL) doesn’t carry over to AVG, which simply skips the blanks; 600 ratings is a large sample, but the customers who didn’t rate may have had different experiences, so 4.2 describes only those who rated.
quiz.learning_outcome: Know who is in an average before you report it: AVG skips NULLs.

modules.title: SQL for real questions: joins and windows
modules.summary: Combine tables with joins, avoid double counting, and compare rows with window functions.
modules.outcome: Combine tables with joins and compare rows with window functions.

learn.title: Joins connect facts to context
learn.body:
An orders table knows each customer_id; a customers table knows their city and sign-up date. A join brings them together, matching rows ON the column they share.

SELECT c.name, o.order_id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id;

An INNER JOIN keeps only rows that match in both tables, so customers with no orders disappear. A LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table (here, customers) and fills the order columns with NULL where nothing matches: that is how you find customers who never ordered. Mind which table is on the left; swap them and you keep every order instead.

One trap: a WHERE condition on the right-hand table, such as WHERE o.order_date >= '2026-04-01', throws away those NULL rows, so the LEFT JOIN quietly acts like an INNER JOIN. Put that condition in the ON clause instead.

learn.title: Watch the row count
learn.body:
A join can multiply rows. Before joining, ask: for each row on my side, how many rows can match on the other? If one customer has three saved addresses and you join orders to addresses, each of that customer’s orders appears three times, and their revenue triples. The query runs without any error, so nothing warns you.

Count the rows, and check a total you trust, before and after every join:

SELECT COUNT(*), SUM(value) FROM orders;

If ₹40 lakh of orders becomes ₹61 lakh after a join, rows were repeated. Fix it by joining to a table with one row per customer (for example, only each customer’s default address), or by summing before you join. The same happens in Excel and pandas: a one-to-many join repeats the “one” side.

learn.title: Number the rows in each group
learn.body:
GROUP BY squashes rows into groups; a window function keeps every row and adds context to it. Inside OVER ( ), PARTITION BY restarts the calculation for each group, and ORDER BY decides which row comes first. ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY paid_at DESC) numbers each user’s payments from the newest:

user 7, 28 April, ₹300 → 1
user 7, 12 April, ₹900 → 2
user 9, 30 April, ₹150 → 1

Keep the rows numbered 1, and you have each user’s latest payment. Without DESC, row 1 is the first payment instead. You can’t filter on a window function in WHERE, because WHERE runs first. Number the rows in a CTE (a named subquery), then filter in the outer query:

WITH numbered AS (SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY paid_at DESC) AS rn FROM payments)
SELECT * FROM numbered WHERE rn = 1;

learn.title: A group’s figure beside every row
learn.body:
AVG(value) OVER (PARTITION BY city) writes each city’s average on every order of that city, so you can compare an order with its own city:

Pune, ₹800 → Pune average ₹600
Pune, ₹400 → ₹600
Kochi, ₹900 → ₹900

With no PARTITION BY, OVER () gives one average for the whole table. Add ORDER BY inside OVER and it becomes a running figure. SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY paid_at) is each user’s running total. LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) puts last month’s revenue beside this month’s. The first month has no earlier row, so its LAG is NULL.

tasks.title: Find the silent customers
tasks.prompt: Tables: customers(customer_id, name, city, signed_up) and orders(order_id, customer_id, order_date, value). Write a query that lists customers who signed up in 2026 but have never ordered. In the playground from module 4, create the two tables and insert: customers (1,'Asha','Pune','2026-01-10'), (2,'Ravi','Kochi','2026-02-03'), (3,'Meena','Jaipur','2025-11-20'), (4,'Imran','Lucknow','2026-03-15'), (5,'Sana','Delhi','2026-03-01'), (6,'Farah','Delhi','2025-12-05'); orders (101,1,'2026-02-01',900), (102,1,'2026-03-05',450), (103,3,'2026-01-12',700), (104,3,'2026-03-20',300), (106,5,'2026-03-25',250). Run your query and paste the result, then run SELECT COUNT(*) on the joined rows before you filter. (About 35 minutes.)
tasks.hint: LEFT JOIN, then keep the rows where the order side is empty. Check: the result is Ravi and Imran. Farah never ordered but signed up in 2025, so the 2026 filter leaves her out; Asha, Meena and Sana have orders. The joined row count before filtering is 8.

tasks.title: First order or repeat?
tasks.prompt: Using the same rows, write and run a query that marks each order as a customer’s first order or a repeat order, then work out what share of March 2026 revenue came from repeat orders. (About 35 minutes.)
tasks.hint: ROW_NUMBER over each customer’s whole order history, by date, in a CTE; filter to March only in the outer query. Check: March has three orders (₹450, ₹300, ₹250). Orders 102 and 104 are repeats, so ₹750 of ₹1,000 is 75%.

reflection.prompt: Have you ever seen a number that was “too good to be true”? Could a join that duplicated rows have explained it?
reflection.hint: Doubled revenue is a classic sign.

quiz.title: Customers who never ordered
quiz.scenario: A meal-kit startup has customers(customer_id, name, city) and orders(order_id, customer_id, order_date).
quiz.question: Which query lists the customers who have never ordered?
options: SELECT c.customer_id FROM customers c INNER JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id WHERE o.order_id IS NULL;
SELECT c.customer_id FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id WHERE o.order_id IS NOT NULL;
SELECT c.customer_id FROM orders o LEFT JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id WHERE o.order_id IS NULL;
SELECT c.customer_id FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id WHERE o.order_id IS NULL;
quiz.explanation: With customers on the left, the LEFT JOIN keeps every customer, and a customer with no orders gets NULL in the order columns, which WHERE o.order_id IS NULL picks out.
quiz.why_wrong: The INNER JOIN drops customers without orders before the filter runs, so it returns nothing; IS NOT NULL keeps the customers who did order, once per order; with orders on the left, every row is an order, so order_id is never NULL and the result is empty.
quiz.learning_outcome: LEFT JOIN from the table you want to keep, then IS NULL, finds what’s missing.

quiz.title: Revenue that grew overnight
quiz.scenario: An analyst joins orders (10,000 rows, ₹82 lakh revenue) to customer_addresses, where some customers have two or three saved addresses. The joined table shows ₹1.3 crore.
quiz.question: What most likely happened?
options: Addresses with no customer linked were added as extra rows, each with an order value
Orders with no saved address were counted twice, once with a blank address row
Orders were repeated once for each of their customer’s addresses, inflating the sum
The ₹82 lakh was for delivered orders only, while the join took in every status
quiz.explanation: A customer with three saved addresses matches three rows, so each of their orders appears three times and its value is summed three times. The query runs without any error.
quiz.why_wrong: A join from orders can’t create rows for addresses that match no order; an order with no address either drops out or appears once with blanks, so it can’t be counted twice; nothing in the case points to a different filter, while customers with several saved addresses explain the rise exactly.
quiz.learning_outcome: Check the row count and a trusted total after every join to catch double counting.

quiz.title: Latest visit per doctor
quiz.scenario: A clinic’s visits table has visit_id, patient_id, visit_date and doctor. The manager wants one row per doctor: that doctor’s most recent visit.
quiz.question: Which expression, kept where it equals 1, picks each doctor’s latest visit?
options: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY doctor ORDER BY visit_date)
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY doctor ORDER BY visit_date DESC)
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY patient_id ORDER BY visit_date DESC)
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY visit_date DESC)
quiz.explanation: PARTITION BY doctor restarts the numbering for each doctor, and ORDER BY visit_date DESC puts the newest visit first, so row 1 is each doctor’s latest visit.
quiz.why_wrong: Ascending order makes row 1 each doctor’s first visit, not the latest; partitioning by patient would give each patient’s latest visit, which suits a list of patients but leaves a doctor with many rows; with no PARTITION BY the numbering runs across all doctors, so only the single latest visit in the whole table is 1.
quiz.learning_outcome: Choose the partition and the sort direction to pick one row per group.

quiz.title: Unusually large orders
quiz.scenario: A furniture brand’s table orders(order_id, city, value) has one row per order. You want to flag orders worth more than three times their own city’s average.
quiz.question: Which expression, added to SELECT, puts each order beside its city’s average order value?
options: AVG(value) OVER (ORDER BY city)
AVG(value) OVER ()
AVG(value) OVER (PARTITION BY order_id)
AVG(value) OVER (PARTITION BY city)
quiz.explanation: PARTITION BY city computes the average within each city and writes it on every order row, without collapsing the rows the way GROUP BY would.
quiz.why_wrong: ORDER BY city without a partition gives a running average over all rows up to that city, so only the first city’s figure is right; an empty OVER () gives the average of all orders, the same on every row; partitioning by order_id averages each order with itself, so every row just shows its own value.
quiz.learning_outcome: Window functions add group context to every row; the partition decides the group.

modules.title: Statistics that change decisions
modules.summary: Variation, samples, bias and A/B tests: tell a real change from noise.
modules.outcome: Use spread, samples and simple experiments to tell a real change from noise.

learn.title: Variation is normal
learn.body:
Daily orders bounce around even when nothing has changed: weekends, salary days, rain, festivals. Before celebrating a jump, compare it with how much the number usually moves. Find its usual range over recent weeks, or its standard deviation (how far values typically sit from the average). If a kirana store’s daily sales have swung between ₹20,000 and ₹27,000 for two months, a ₹26,000 day is ordinary, and even ₹28,000 is only a hint.

Compare like with like: this Saturday with recent Saturdays, not with a Tuesday. One day outside the usual range is worth watching, not announcing. A change that lasts a week or more, ideally beside stores that didn’t change anything, is much stronger evidence. The same thinking applies to dashboard targets and alerts.

learn.title: Samples, margins and who answered
learn.body:
A survey of 200 students isn’t every student. The smaller the sample, the wider the range around the result. Say “72% are satisfied” comes from 50 answers. For all students, it could be anywhere from about 60% to 84%. From 2,000 answers, it is within a couple of points. In the same way, a 5.0 rating from 6 reviews tells you less than 4.4 stars from 3,000 reviews.

Size doesn’t fix who answered, though. Perhaps only happy customers reply. Or you ask the people who stayed, and not those who left. Then the result is biased. A bigger sample just gives the same wrong answer more confidently. Ask three questions: who was asked, who replied, and who is missing? A sample picked at random from everyone is the fair way to describe a whole group.

learn.title: A/B tests answer “did it work?”
learn.body:
Split users at random: half see the old checkout, half the new one, at the same time. Random assignment balances everything else on average (cities, devices, keen and casual users), so a clear difference can be credited to the change. Random sampling decides who is in the study; random assignment decides who gets which version.

Before you start, fix the measure, sample size and length, covering whole weeks. Checking every hour and stopping the moment it “looks good” fools you, because early leads swing by chance.

For example, a Jaipur tutoring app split 8,000 new users at random for two full weeks: 4,000 saw the old checkout and 4,000 the new one. 160 (4.0%) and 200 (5.0%) paid.

learn.title: Reading the result
learn.body:
A significance test tells you whether a gap is bigger than chance usually makes. A free online A/B test calculator says that 4.0% against 5.0%, with 4,000 users in each group, would happen by chance only about 3 times in 100: a real difference. 4.0% against 4.3% would happen by chance about half the time, so it shows nothing either way.

A result that isn’t significant doesn’t prove there is no effect; the test may be too small to see it. If a test runs its planned length with no clear difference, don’t extend it until one appears: decide on other grounds, such as cost or simplicity. And “significant” means unlikely to be chance, not big or important.

tasks.title: Design a test
tasks.prompt: An edtech app wants to know whether a ₹99 first-month offer brings more paid sign-ups than a 7-day free trial. Design an A/B test: who is in it, how they are split, what you measure, how long it runs, and what result would make you pick a winner. (About 25 minutes.)
tasks.hint: What could go wrong if the offer ran only in one city, or only in the first week? Check: a good design splits users at random between both offers over the same two or more whole weeks. It measures paid sign-ups per user, and picks a winner only if a significance test says the gap is not chance.

tasks.title: Noise or signal?
tasks.prompt: A shop’s daily sales were between ₹38,000 and ₹52,000 for the last 60 days. Yesterday, after a new shelf layout, sales were ₹54,000. Write what you would tell the owner, and what you would check before concluding that the layout worked. (About 20 minutes.)
tasks.hint: One day against a pattern. Check: ₹54,000 is just above the usual top of ₹52,000, a gap of ₹2,000 on a range of ₹14,000. Say it is a hint, not proof, and watch a week or two of Saturdays against recent ones.

reflection.prompt: When have you seen a survey or “study” quoted that you now doubt? What would you want to know about how it was done?
reflection.hint: How many people, who were they, and who chose them?

quiz.title: The new onboarding screen
quiz.scenario: An edtech app is testing a new onboarding screen. For each new user, the app decides at random whether they see the old screen or the new one.
quiz.question: Why does the app assign users at random, instead of letting them choose or splitting by city?
options: So both groups end up with exactly the same mix of cities, ages and devices
So the result can be applied to every user of the app, not only those in the test
So each group is large enough to give a statistically significant result
So other differences even out on average, and a gap can be put down to the screen
quiz.explanation: When chance decides who sees which screen, keen and casual users, cities and devices spread across both groups on average, so a clear difference in results can be credited to the screen itself.
quiz.why_wrong: Random assignment balances groups on average, not exactly, which is why a test still needs a check against chance; applying the result to everyone depends on who is in the study (random sampling), not on how they are split; group size decides whether a gap can be detected, and randomising doesn’t change it.
quiz.learning_outcome: Random assignment is what lets a test credit a difference to the change.

quiz.title: Two app ratings
quiz.scenario: You are choosing an expense-tracking app to recommend to your college’s students. App A shows 4.9 stars from 40 reviews. App B shows 4.6 stars from 52,000 reviews.
quiz.question: Which rating is the more reliable guide to what a new user will think?
options: App A’s, because a 0.3-star gap is large on a 5-point scale
Both, equally, once you look at the share of 5-star reviews in each
App B’s: an average from 40 reviews could shift a lot with a few more
Neither: reviews are self-selected, so both averages are equally biased
quiz.explanation: With 40 reviews, a handful of new ones can move the average a lot; 52,000 reviews pin it down closely. App B’s 4.6 is the more dependable estimate.
quiz.why_wrong: A 0.3-star gap would matter if both averages were reliable, but 40 reviews can’t show it is real; the share of 5-star reviews comes from the same 40 reviews, so it is just as uncertain; self-selection can bias both, but nothing shows it biases them equally, and the sample size still decides which average is steadier.
quiz.learning_outcome: Small samples give uncertain results: ask how many answers sit behind a figure.

quiz.title: The early winner
quiz.scenario: A team checks its A/B test every hour, and stops it on day 2 because the new design is ahead by 9%.
quiz.question: What should the team have done instead?
options: Fixed the measure and a length of whole weeks before starting, and judged it only at the end
Kept checking hourly, but stopped only once the lead passed a significance test at 95%
Stopped only after the new design had stayed more than 9% ahead for 24 hours in a row
Checked once a day instead of every hour, so short swings even out before they decide
quiz.explanation: Early leads swing by chance, and checking often while ready to stop gives chance many tries to produce a lead. Deciding the measure and the length (whole weeks) in advance, and judging once at the end, removes that.
quiz.why_wrong: A significance test checked every hour is still peeking: with many checks, one will pass by chance; a lead that lasts 24 hours on day 2 is still an early swing; checking daily means fewer peeks, but stopping at the first good day is the same mistake.
quiz.learning_outcome: Fix a test’s measure and length before it starts, and judge it at the end.

quiz.title: The satisfied members
quiz.scenario: A gym chain emailed a survey to 3,000 members picked at random from all 20,000, including those who left this year. Its scale was balanced: very satisfied, satisfied, dissatisfied, very dissatisfied. 400 replied (13%), most of them members of five years or more, and 90% of the replies were “very satisfied”. The CEO wants “90% of our members are very satisfied” in an advert.
quiz.question: What is the main problem with the claim?
options: Only current members were asked, so those who quit this year are missing from it
400 replies are too few to describe a chain of 20,000 members with any precision
The answer scale leans positive, which pushes replies towards “very satisfied”
Only 13% replied, mostly long-time members, so the 90% speaks for the keenest
quiz.explanation: The 3,000 were picked fairly, but only 13% replied, and most replies came from members of five years or more, who are the likeliest to be happy. Who replied, not who was asked, is the flaw here, so 90% describes the keenest members, not all of them.
quiz.why_wrong: Asking only current members would be the flaw if those who left had been left out, but the 3,000 were drawn from everyone, leavers included; too few replies would be the problem with about 40 answers, but 400 gives a margin of roughly ±3 points; a lopsided scale would tilt the answers, but this one has two positive and two negative choices.
quiz.learning_outcome: Check who was asked, who replied and who is missing; the flaw is wherever the facts point.

modules.title: Python and pandas for analysis
modules.summary: Load, clean, summarise and join data with pandas, and check each step.
modules.outcome: Load, clean, summarise and join data with pandas in a notebook.

learn.title: Why Python when there’s Excel?
learn.body:
Python repeats your steps exactly on next month’s file, handles millions of rows, and records every step in a notebook anyone can rerun. pandas is its table library: a DataFrame is a sheet you can program, with named columns and one row per record.

You can run it free in Google Colab, in your browser, with pandas already installed. It also opens in a phone’s browser, which is enough for this module’s short tasks; a laptop or a college computer is easier for longer work. Python in Excel also works, if your Microsoft 365 plan includes it. A notebook mixes code cells with their results, so you run one step, look, then write the next. Start like this:

import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("orders.csv")

pandas 3.0 (January 2026) changed a few things. The one beginners meet first: to change some values, write df.loc[rows, "column"] = value. The chained form df["column"][rows] = value no longer changes df.

learn.title: Filter and total, worked through
learn.body:
Priya has five orders: Pune ₹500, Pune ₹700, Kochi ₹400, Pune ₹300 (failed), Kochi ₹600.

ok = df[df["status"] == "success"]
ok.groupby("city")["value"].sum()

This prints Kochi 1000 and Pune 1200. With .count() instead, it prints Kochi 2 and Pune 2: rows, not rupees.

To combine two conditions, put each one in its own brackets, and use & for and, | for or:

df[(df["status"] == "success") & (df["amount"] > 5000)]

Python’s own words and and or don’t work on whole columns. Without brackets, & runs before == and >, so pandas usually stops with an error.

learn.title: Join and read dates
learn.body:
df.merge(customers, on="customer_id", how="left") joins two tables. how="left" keeps every order. For example, an order with a guest customer_id keeps its row, with NaN (empty) in the city column. Without how="left", merge keeps only the orders that match a customer.

pd.to_datetime(df["order_date"], dayfirst=True) reads day-first dates. dayfirst=True reads 05/04/2026 as 5 April, but it is a preference, not a rule. format="%d/%m/%Y" is stricter: it stops with an error on any date in another format. Check the result with a date you know.

learn.title: Check as you go
learn.body:
df.info() and df.describe() profile a DataFrame: column types, blanks, minimum and maximum. After every step, look at the shape (df.shape gives rows and columns), a few rows (df.head()) and a total you know. Write the checks into the notebook so they run every time:

print(df.shape, df["amount"].sum())

If the row count or the revenue changes after a merge, rows were duplicated: some keys appear more than once in the other table. After a filter, ask whether the number of rows you kept is believable. After drop_duplicates, look at a few of the rows it removed: dropping on one column, such as a name or a phone number, can delete real, different people.

Leave a short comment (a line starting with #) saying why each step exists. Next month, you will be the person who needs it.

tasks.title: Run your first notebook
tasks.prompt:
In Google Colab (free, in a browser), make a new notebook and paste:
import pandas as pd, io
csv = '''txn_id,merchant_category,amount,txn_time,status
1,Grocery,450,05/05/2026 10:15,success
2,Travel,5200,12/05/2026 18:40,success
3,Grocery,300,13/05/2026 09:00,failed
4,Food,800,20/05/2026 21:05,success
5,Travel,2500,30/04/2026 23:50,success
6,Food,650,31/05/2026 20:00,success'''
df = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(csv))
Then find May 2026’s merchant categories by the value of successful transactions, highest first. Print df.shape after each step. (About 40 minutes.)
tasks.hint: The dates are day-first. What does 12/05/2026 become if pandas reads it month-first? After pd.to_datetime(df["txn_time"], dayfirst=True), df["txn_time"].dt.month == 5 picks May; .sort_values(ascending=False) puts the largest first. Check: Travel 5,200, Food 1,450, Grocery 450. The 30 April Travel payment and the failed Grocery one are left out.

tasks.title: Read the code
tasks.prompt:
Explain what this code does, line by line, and one thing that could go wrong:
df = pd.read_csv("leads.csv")
df = df.drop_duplicates(subset="phone")
df["source"] = df["source"].str.strip().str.lower()
summary = df.groupby("source").size().sort_values(ascending=False)
Then run it in Colab on these six leads (read them with io.StringIO as in task 1), and say how many leads it drops, and whether they were really duplicates:
lead_id,name,phone,source
1,Asha Nair,9811100001, Instagram
2,Ravi Das,9811100002,Google
3,Meena Rao,9811100003,instagram
4,Rohan Rao,9811100003,Instagram
5,Imran Khan,9811100005,GOOGLE
6,Sana Khan,9811100006,Google
(About 30 minutes.)
tasks.hint: Are two leads with the same phone number always the same person? Check: it drops 1 lead, Rohan, who shares a family phone with Meena and is a different person. The summary shows google 3 and instagram 2; without the drop, instagram would be 3.

tasks.title: Join and check
tasks.prompt: Using the data from task 1, make a merchants table with three rows: Grocery, Asha; Travel, Ravi; Travel, Meena (columns merchant_category and manager). Build the merchants table the way task 1 built the transactions: paste it as text and read it with pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(...)). Merge it into the transactions with how="left". Print the shape and the total amount before and after, then fix the merge so the total matches again. (About 30 minutes.)
tasks.hint: Which category appears twice in merchants? Check: the shape goes from (6, 5) to (8, 6) and the total from 9,900 to 17,600, because both Travel rows repeat. Keep one row per category (for example drop_duplicates on merchant_category) and the total is 9,900 again.

reflection.prompt: What repetitive data task would you most like to automate? List the steps a script would follow.
reflection.hint: Anything you do every week in the same order is a candidate.

quiz.title: Total per outlet
quiz.scenario: df holds a bakery chain’s sales, one row per sale, with the columns sale_id, outlet and sales (₹).
quiz.question: Which line gives the total sales for each outlet?
options: df.groupby("outlet")["sales"].sum()
df.groupby("outlet")["sales"].count()
df.groupby("outlet")["sales"].mean()
df.groupby("sales")["outlet"].sum()
quiz.explanation: groupby("outlet") makes one group per outlet; selecting "sales" and summing adds up each outlet’s sales.
quiz.why_wrong: .count() gives the number of sales per outlet, not their value; .mean() gives the average sale per outlet; grouping by sales and summing outlet swaps the two columns and joins outlet names together.
quiz.learning_outcome: groupby the category, select the number, then pick the right aggregate.

quiz.title: Indian dates in pandas
quiz.scenario: A column holds dates written the Indian way, such as "08/02/2026" for 8 February 2026.
quiz.question: Which line reads them correctly as dates?
options: pd.to_datetime(df["date"], errors="coerce")
pd.to_datetime(df["date"], dayfirst=True)
df["date"].astype("datetime64[ns]")
pd.to_datetime(df["date"], format="%m/%d/%Y")
quiz.explanation: dayfirst=True tells pandas the first number is the day, so 08/02/2026 is read as 8 February. Without it, pandas can read an ambiguous date like this month-first, as 2 August. format="%d/%m/%Y" is stricter still: it fails loudly on any date in another format.
quiz.why_wrong: errors="coerce" only blanks dates it can’t read, and astype also reads 08/02 month-first, so February and August still swap; the format %m/%d/%Y says the month comes first, the wrong way round.
quiz.learning_outcome: Tell pandas the dates are day-first (dayfirst=True), or give the exact format (format="%d/%m/%Y"), which is strict.

quiz.title: Removed coupon codes
quiz.scenario: orders has 12,000 rows. 150 of them carry a coupon_code that was removed from the coupons table last month, so it isn’t in coupons.
quiz.question: After orders.merge(coupons, on="coupon_code", how="left"), what happens to those 150 orders?
options: They are kept, with the coupon columns empty (NaN)
They are dropped, as they have nothing to match in coupons
They are kept, with the coupon columns filled with 0 or ""
The merge stops with an error naming the unmatched coupon_codes
quiz.explanation: A left merge keeps every row of the left table, here orders; unmatched rows get NaN, meaning missing, in the coupons columns. The result still has 12,000 rows.
quiz.why_wrong: Dropping unmatched rows is what an inner merge (the default) does; pandas marks the gaps as missing (NaN), not as 0 or empty text, because missing isn’t zero; unmatched keys are normal in a merge, so pandas raises no error.
quiz.learning_outcome: Choose the merge type for the rows you must keep, and expect NaN where nothing matches.

quiz.title: Pune fares above ₹800
quiz.scenario: df holds a month of cab bookings with the columns booking_id, city and fare (₹).
quiz.question: Which line keeps only Pune bookings with a fare above ₹800?
options: df[(df["city"] == "Pune") & (df["fare"] > 800)]
df[(df["city"] == "Pune") and (df["fare"] > 800)]
df[df["city"] == "Pune" & df["fare"] > 800]
df[(df["city"] == "Pune") | (df["fare"] > 800)]
quiz.explanation: pandas combines conditions on whole columns with & (and) and | (or), and each condition needs its own brackets.
quiz.why_wrong: Python’s own and works on single values, not whole columns, so pandas raises an error; without brackets, & is applied before == and >, so pandas raises an error instead of filtering; | means “or”, which would also keep Pune bookings at any fare and other cities’ bookings above ₹800.
quiz.learning_outcome: Combine pandas conditions with & or |, each condition in its own brackets.

modules.title: Dashboards people use
modules.summary: Choose the right chart, design dashboards around decisions, and check what Copilot drafts.
modules.outcome: Choose the right chart and build a dashboard around the decisions it supports.

learn.title: Pick the chart for the question
learn.body:
Change over time: a line chart, with time running left to right. Comparing categories: a bar chart, sorted, and horizontal if the names are long. Part of a whole: a stacked bar, or a pie for two or three parts only. Relationship between two numbers: a scatter plot. How one number is spread (how many orders of each size): a histogram. When people need exact values, a well-formatted table is fine.

Bars are read by their length, so a bar chart’s axis starts at zero. If sales rise from ₹100 lakh to ₹103 lakh and the axis starts at ₹99 lakh, the bars are 1 and 4 units long: a 3% rise looks like four times as much. A line chart may start higher, as long as the axis is labelled, because readers judge its slope, not its height. Avoid 3D effects and rainbow colours: they make values harder to compare.

learn.title: A dashboard answers three questions
learn.body:
Are we on track (the key number against its target)? Where is the problem (a breakdown by city, channel or product)? What changed (the trend against last period)? Put the most important number top left, keep each page to one purpose, and use colour only to draw attention to what needs action: a city below target turns red, and everything else stays grey.

Show every key number beside something to compare it with: a target, last month, or the same week last year. “On-time deliveries: 87%” means little; “87% against a 92% target, down from 90% last week” tells the manager to act. Before you build, ask the people who will use it which decisions they make each week, and drop any chart that doesn’t feed one. Power BI Desktop, Looker Studio and Excel all do this free.

learn.title: Power BI in practice
learn.body:
Power BI Desktop is free for Windows. It connects to Excel, databases and files, and builds an interactive report on a data model. Measures written in DAX, such as

Revenue = SUM(Orders[Value])

are reused across visuals, and visual calculations add running totals or moving averages inside a chart. Sharing reports online with colleagues needs a paid licence, which employers usually provide.

Copilot in Power BI can draft measures and pages, but it needs a paid capacity your employer provides. On your own, build the measure in free Power BI Desktop, and use a free AI assistant to draft or explain the DAX: the checking step is the same. Whoever drafts it, read the DAX, check that its definition and period match what you meant, and test its numbers against a total you trust before sharing.

tasks.title: Build the weekly page
tasks.prompt: Here is one week for 8 pharmacy stores, as sales against target in ₹ lakh: S01 4.2/4.0, S02 3.1/3.5, S03 5.6/5.0, S04 2.7/3.0, S05 3.9/4.0, S06 6.1/5.5, S07 2.2/2.5, S08 4.8/4.5. In Google Sheets (free, also in the phone app) or Looker Studio, build one page with: the chain’s total against its target at the top; a bar chart of each store’s % of target, sorted, with stores below 100% in red; and one line saying which store managers the regional manager should call. Share a screenshot or link. (About 35 minutes.)
tasks.hint: Work out % of target for each store first. Which four are below 100%? Check: the total is ₹32.6 lakh against ₹32 lakh (102%). S07, S02, S04 and S05 are below target, so those are the managers to call, S07 first.

tasks.title: Fix a bad chart
tasks.prompt: Describe a chart you have seen that was hard to read (a 3D pie, too many colours, an axis that doesn’t start at zero). Explain what was wrong, and how you would redraw it. Then redraw it in Google Sheets from made-up numbers and share both versions. (About 35 minutes.)
tasks.hint: Would a sorted bar chart say it more clearly? Check: a good redraw is a sorted bar chart with an axis from zero, one highlight colour, and a title that states the point.

reflection.prompt: Which number at your college, job or home would be worth tracking on a dashboard? What would you do differently if it went down?
reflection.hint: A good dashboard number leads to an action.

quiz.title: Eighteen months of revenue
quiz.scenario: The founder of a Jaipur handicrafts brand wants to repeat her best campaigns next year. She asks you which three of the last 18 months brought the most revenue.
quiz.question: Which chart answers her best?
options: A bar chart of the 18 months, sorted from highest revenue to lowest
A line chart of the 18 months, running left to right in time order
A histogram of the 18 monthly revenue figures, grouped into ranges
A table of the 18 months in time order, with exact ₹ figures for each
quiz.explanation: She wants to rank the months, so sorted bars put the three biggest at the top, where they can be read at a glance.
quiz.why_wrong: A line chart in time order is right for how revenue has moved over time, but she must hunt along it for the three highest points; a histogram is right for how often a month reaches each revenue level, but it hides which months they were; an exact table suits a budget that needs the figures, but in time order she still has to scan all 18 rows to find the top three.
quiz.learning_outcome: Pick the chart for the question: sorted bars to rank, a line for a trend.

quiz.title: The giant jump
quiz.scenario: A bar chart shows this quarter’s sales at ₹210 lakh against ₹200 lakh last quarter, but the new bar looks six times taller.
quiz.question: What is most likely wrong?
options: The value axis starts near ₹198 lakh instead of zero, exaggerating a 5% rise
The bars are drawn in 3D, so the nearer bar looks larger than the further one
The axis uses a log scale, which stretches small differences near the top
Nothing: the bars are drawn to scale, and 5% is simply a strong quarter
quiz.explanation: Bars are read by their length. With the axis starting at ₹198 lakh, the bars are 12 and 2 units long, so a 5% rise looks like 500%.
quiz.why_wrong: 3D effects can distort a little, but not turn a 5% gap into a sixfold one; a log scale squeezes large values together rather than stretching small gaps; drawn to scale from zero, ₹210 lakh and ₹200 lakh would look almost the same height.
quiz.learning_outcome: Start a bar chart’s axis at zero.

quiz.title: The 30-minute promise
quiz.scenario: A food-delivery company’s target is 95% of orders delivered within 30 minutes in every city. Each morning its operations head opens the dashboard to decide which city managers to call about missing that target.
quiz.question: What should the top of the dashboard show?
options: Each city’s count of late orders this week, highest first, the top three in red
The national % of orders within 30 minutes against 95%, with a 12-week trend
Each city’s average delivery time against 30 minutes, cities above it in red
Each city’s % of orders within 30 minutes against 95%, cities below it in red
quiz.explanation: The target is a rate (95% of orders within 30 minutes) and the decision is which city manager to call, so the top shows that rate for each city against 95%, with the cities below it in red.
quiz.why_wrong: A count of late orders is right for sending extra riders where the volume of late orders is, but it mostly ranks the busiest cities, not those missing the rate; the national figure with a trend suits a CEO’s monthly review, but it can’t say which city to call; an average delivery time would fit a target set as an average, but an average can be under 30 minutes while far fewer than 95% of orders arrive on time.
quiz.learning_outcome: Build the top of a dashboard around its user’s decision: the target’s own measure, by group.

quiz.title: Two repeat rates
quiz.scenario: At work, Copilot in Power BI (on your employer’s paid capacity) drafts a Repeat Customer Rate measure. Its DAX counts this quarter’s customers who have two or more orders ever, out of all this quarter’s customers: 74%. Your SQL counts this quarter’s customers who ordered before the quarter began: 41%. The marketing head, who owns the dashboard, defines a repeat customer as one who ordered before this quarter. She wants one repeat-customer rate on the page.
quiz.question: What should go on the dashboard?
options: Keep the 74% measure, and relabel it “customers with two or more orders ever”
Show both figures side by side, each with a note that gives its definition
Type the 41% from your SQL into a text box, and delete the DAX measure
Change the DAX to the marketing head’s definition, and check it returns 41%
quiz.explanation: The two figures differ because they use two definitions: the DAX counts a new customer who ordered twice this quarter as a repeat. The dashboard’s owner has defined the term, so fix the measure to that definition and check it matches the SQL’s 41%.
quiz.why_wrong: Relabelling the 74% would be right if the marketing head wanted lifetime loyalty, but her definition is ordering before the quarter; two figures with notes suit two teams that use two agreed definitions, but here there is one owner and one definition; a typed-in number could do for a one-off slide, but a dashboard refreshes, so it would be wrong by next quarter.
quiz.learning_outcome: Reconcile an AI-drafted measure with the business’s own definition, then check it.

modules.title: AI as your analysis partner
modules.summary: Prompt AI assistants well, check everything they produce, and keep personal data safe.
modules.outcome: Use AI assistants to speed up analysis, and check their work before anyone relies on it.

learn.title: What AI is good at
learn.body:
AI assistants draft SQL and pandas code from a plain-English question. They also explain formulas, suggest cleaning steps and summarise findings. Copilot in Excel does this, depending on your Microsoft plan. So do ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini, which have free plans.

Give context: table and column names, what each column means, business terms, the period, and which database you use (PostgreSQL, MySQL), as each writes SQL a little differently. Otherwise it guesses silently. Ask it to explain its code line by line.

Worked example. Arjun, at a Kochi furniture store, asked: “PostgreSQL. Table orders(order_id, city, order_time, value), one row per order; order_time is a timestamp. Total value by city for March 2026. Explain each line.” It returned:
SELECT city, SUM(value) FROM orders WHERE order_time BETWEEN '2026-03-01' AND '2026-03-31' GROUP BY city;
His PivotTable showed Kochi at ₹8,40,000; the query said ₹8,12,000. It stopped at midnight on 31 March. He changed it to order_time < '2026-04-01', and the totals matched.

learn.title: Where it goes wrong
learn.body:
AI can write code that runs but answers a different question. It can invent column names it has never seen, mishandle dates or missing values, and state wrong numbers confidently. Microsoft’s own guidance on Copilot in Excel says it can make mistakes and asks you to verify what it creates.

Treat its output like a new colleague’s first draft. Read it, and check that its definition and period match yours. Then work out one result another way, such as a PivotTable for one month you know. Compare totals with a source you trust.

Some checks feel safe but aren’t. Code that runs without errors can still be wrong. Running it again gives the same wrong answer. A second assistant gives another opinion, not proof. And a number in its usual range can still rest on the wrong definition.

learn.title: Protect people’s data
learn.body:
Don’t paste personal data into public AI tools: names, phone numbers, Aadhaar numbers or health details. India’s Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 sets the rules. Personal data may be used only for a lawful purpose. That needs the person’s consent, or one of a few uses the Act permits. The data must also be kept safe. Use the tools your organisation approves. Otherwise, share only column names and a few made-up rows. Then run the resulting code on the real data yourself.

Some shortcuts don’t make it safe. A paid plan doesn’t. Switching chat history off doesn’t. Nor does swapping names for initials while phone numbers and diagnoses stay in. A phone number alone can point to one person. Two questions matter: is this use allowed, and does the data stay protected? The tool’s settings don’t answer them.

tasks.title: Write a good prompt
