tasks.prompt: You need the share of repeat customers in each month, from tables orders(order_id, customer_id, order_date, value) and customers(customer_id, city, signed_up). Write the prompt you would give an AI assistant to draft the SQL, then list three checks you would run on what it returns. Give your prompt to a free AI assistant (ChatGPT, Gemini or Claude all have free plans) with only the column names and the made-up rows from module 5’s playground: never real customer data. Run the SQL it returns in that playground, and check March by hand. Hand in your prompt, its SQL, your check and whether they matched. (About 35 minutes.)
tasks.hint: Define “repeat customer” in the prompt, or the assistant will choose a definition for you. Check: with module 5’s rows, March has three ordering customers, and two of them (Asha and Meena) ordered before, so the share is 2 of 3, about 67%. If the SQL gives something else, find which definition it used.

tasks.title: Catch the error
tasks.prompt: An AI assistant summarises a sales file: “Revenue grew 40% in Q2, driven by Chennai.” Describe how you would check both parts of that sentence before putting it in a report. (About 25 minutes.)
tasks.hint: Recalculate from the raw data, and check which dates it used for Q2.

reflection.prompt: Where would you trust an AI assistant fully, and where would you always check its work? Why the difference?
reflection.hint: Think about the cost of a mistake in each case.

quiz.title: The repeat-customer prompt
quiz.scenario: You want each 2026 month’s share of repeat customers from your company’s orders table, and a free AI assistant to draft the SQL. The company uses PostgreSQL.
quiz.question: Which prompt is most likely to get correct SQL?
options: “Table orders(order_id, customer_id, order_date, value). Write SQL for the repeat customer rate in each month of 2026, efficient and readable.”
“Table orders(order_id, customer_id, order_date, value). For each 2026 month, what % of that month’s customers had ordered before it? PostgreSQL.”
“In our data, a repeat customer is one who has ordered before. Write PostgreSQL for each 2026 month’s repeat customer rate from the orders table.”
“You are a senior PostgreSQL analyst. Write efficient, well-commented SQL for the repeat customer rate in each month of 2026 from our orders table.”
quiz.explanation: It gives the table and its columns, defines exactly who counts (that month’s customers with an order before that month), sets the period and names the database, so the assistant has nothing important to guess.
quiz.why_wrong: The schema-only prompt leaves “repeat customer rate” undefined and names no dialect; the prompt with a definition defines a repeat customer but names no columns, so the assistant must invent them; the expert persona sounds strong but gives no columns and no definition of a repeat customer.
quiz.learning_outcome: Give an AI assistant the schema, the definition, the period and the tool.

quiz.title: Code that runs
quiz.scenario: Your orders file has one row for each item in an order, so an order_id repeats once per item. AI-written pandas code averages the file’s value column, runs without errors, and reports an average order value of ₹1,240 for the year.
quiz.question: Which check shows whether ₹1,240 is the average order value?
options: Total the value column, and divide it by the number of distinct order_ids
Recompute one month’s average of the value column in a PivotTable, and compare
Check that ₹1,240 sits inside your usual ₹1,100–1,400 range for orders
Rerun the code on a fresh export of the file, and compare the two results
quiz.explanation: Each row is an item, so averaging the value column gives the average item value, not the average order. Dividing the total by the number of distinct orders gives the average order value, and shows at once whether ₹1,240 is right.
quiz.why_wrong: A PivotTable is an independent tool, but averaging the same item-level column there repeats the same mistake, so it would agree with the wrong figure; the usual range is a good check for a units slip, such as paise read as rupees, but an item average can still land inside it; a fresh export would matter if the file might have changed since the run, but the same code on the same rows gives the same answer.
quiz.learning_outcome: A check is only independent if it uses the right definition, at the right level of the data.

quiz.title: The patient list
quiz.scenario: You want an AI assistant’s help cleaning a list of 20,000 patients with names, phone numbers and diagnoses.
quiz.question: What is the right approach?
options: Delete the names and diagnoses, keep the phone numbers, and paste it into a free chatbot
Use a chatbot whose settings say your data won’t be used for training, and paste in the full list
Use a tool your organisation approves, or share only column names and made-up rows
Share a random sample of 500 rows instead of all 20,000, so fewer patients are exposed
quiz.explanation: Health and contact details are personal data, and the law asks whether this use is allowed and the data kept safe. An approved tool, or the structure with made-up rows (then running the code yourself on the real data), gets the help without exposing anyone.
quiz.why_wrong: A phone number alone can point to one person, so removing names and diagnoses doesn’t make the list anonymous; a no-training setting is a promise about the tool, not an answer to whether your organisation allows this use and whether the data stays protected; 500 patients’ health data is still personal data.
quiz.learning_outcome: Keep personal data out of unapproved AI tools; share structure, not people.

quiz.title: The column that isn’t there
quiz.scenario: You described your tables to an AI assistant in one sentence, but never pasted their definitions. The SQL it wrote refers to customers.lifetime_value, a column that doesn’t exist in your database.
quiz.question: What should you do?
options: Ask it again, telling it to use only columns that exist, then re-check the query it returns
Give it the real table definitions, then re-check the whole query it returns
Swap in total_spent, the nearest real column, and run the query as it stands
Fix that one reference, and trust the result if the row counts look sensible
quiz.explanation: The assistant never saw your schema, so it guessed, and the invented column shows that other parts may be guesses too. Give it the real table definitions, then check the whole query, not just the line that failed.
quiz.why_wrong: Asking it to use only existing columns would be right if it already had the definitions and overlooked one, but it never saw them, so it can only guess again, and a re-check would just find more guesses; swapping in total_spent would be right if your data dictionary defines it as lifetime spend and you had checked the rest of the query, but neither is true yet; sensible row counts can’t show the logic is right.
quiz.learning_outcome: An invented detail means re-checking the whole AI answer, with the real schema.

modules.title: From numbers to decisions
modules.summary: Lead with the recommendation, turn findings into actions, and be honest about limits.
modules.outcome: Turn an analysis into a clear recommendation a manager can act on.

learn.title: Lead with the answer
learn.body:
Start with the recommendation and the number behind it. For example: “Move ₹2 lakh from Meta to Google Search in Pune: Search brings customers at ₹310 each against ₹780 on Meta.” Then the evidence, then the caveats. Busy managers often read only the first lines before deciding whether to read on.

A good opening is specific about the action, its scope (which cities, which products, from when) and its size in ₹. Compare two weaker openings. “Returns are a growing concern, so we should review our policy” names no action and no number. “We analysed 14 months of orders across 6 cities” describes your work, not the answer. Keep the method for later in the memo, or an appendix. Write the first line as if it were the only one your manager will read.

learn.title: So what, and now what?
learn.body:
For every chart, say what it shows and what it means. “Returns are 18% for cash-on-delivery orders and 6% for UPI” is a finding. “Offering ₹30 off for paying by UPI could cut returns” is the insight, with an action.

Watch two traps. First, a share isn’t a rate. “Pune has 40% of all late deliveries” may only mean Pune has most deliveries. So compare the late rate (late ÷ all deliveries) in each city. Second, a pattern isn’t proof of cause. Customers who join a loyalty scheme may spend more because they were already keener. So suggest a test before a big change.

Where you can, put a value on the action: extra sales × your margin, minus what it costs, measured against a similar group that didn’t get it. For example, ₹10 lakh of extra sales at a 40% margin is ₹4 lakh of profit; minus a ₹1.5 lakh cost, the action made ₹2.5 lakh.

learn.title: Be honest about uncertainty
learn.body:
State the period, the data source, the sample size and what you couldn’t check. Two weeks of data from the IPL season may not describe a normal month: say so, and say when you will re-check. Whether data is typical depends on the decision. Three Diwali weeks are poor evidence for a normal month. But they are the right evidence for planning next Diwali. A recommendation with clear limits earns more trust than a confident one that later falls apart. It also tells the reader what to watch next.

Be honest without burying the answer. Give the recommendation first, then the one or two limits that matter to the decision, not a list of every possible doubt. “Based on 9,000 orders from March to August; monsoon months may differ, so we will compare September” is enough. If a limit is serious enough to change the decision, propose a small test or pilot instead of a full roll-out.

tasks.title: Write the first paragraph
tasks.prompt: You found that a D2C skincare brand’s customers who start with the trial kit are 2.3 times more likely to buy again within 60 days than customers who start with a full-size product (14,000 customers, January–June 2026). Write the opening paragraph of a memo to the founder, with your recommendation.
tasks.hint: Recommendation first, evidence second, one honest caveat.

tasks.title: Turn findings into actions
tasks.prompt: Three findings from a college canteen’s sales data: 60% of sales happen between 12:30 and 1:30 pm; the queue takes 14 minutes at peak; 30% of students who arrive at peak leave without buying. Write one insight and one action for each finding.
tasks.hint: What could the canteen change by next week?

reflection.prompt: Think of a presentation or message that persuaded you. What did the person do that you could use in your own reports?
reflection.hint: Notice what came first, and what they left out.

quiz.title: The returns update
quiz.scenario: An online fashion store sells ₹60 lakh a month in Tier-3 cities, and 70% of those orders are cash on delivery (COD). Tier-3 COD orders are returned at 31%, costing about ₹4 lakh a month; elsewhere COD is returned at 10%, close to prepaid orders. Last quarter a ₹49 COD fee ran for eight weeks in six Tier-3 cities picked at random: COD returns there fell to 19%, while orders were only 2% lower than in the other Tier-3 cities.
quiz.question: Which opening line should your update to the operations head use?
options: “Recommendation: add the ₹49 COD fee in every Tier-3 city, where COD returns cost about ₹4 lakh a month.”
“Recommendation: pause cash on delivery in Tier-3 cities, where COD returns cost about ₹4 lakh a month.”
“Recommendation: pause cash on delivery in every city, as COD orders are returned more often than prepaid ones.”
“Recommendation: test a ₹49 COD fee in two Tier-3 cities for a month, before deciding for the rest of the tier.”
quiz.explanation: COD is 70% of Tier-3 sales, about ₹42 lakh a month, so pausing it risks far more than the ₹4 lakh of returns. A random trial in six Tier-3 cities has already shown the fee cutting COD returns from 31% to 19% for 2% fewer orders, so extending it to every Tier-3 city is the specific, scoped action the evidence supports.
quiz.why_wrong: Pausing COD in Tier-3 would be right if COD were a small share of Tier-3 sales, but at 70% it puts about ₹42 lakh of monthly sales at risk to save ₹4 lakh; pausing it everywhere would be right if returns were high in every tier, but outside Tier-3 COD returns are 10%, close to prepaid; a test first would be right if the fee were untried in Tier-3 cities, but the random six-city trial has already shown how Tier-3 customers react.
quiz.learning_outcome: Lead with the specific action the facts support, with its scope and its ₹ impact.

quiz.title: The insights slide
quiz.scenario: You are writing the “insights” slide of a snack brand’s quarterly review. Of 1,000 carts started last quarter, 930 got past login, 850 past the address step, 760 past the delivery-fee step, and 340 completed payment.
quiz.question: Which line is the insight, with an action, that the slide should lead with?
options: “Most carts are lost at login; letting shoppers check out as guests could cut that.”
“Most carts are lost at payment; offering one-tap UPI at that step could cut that.”
“Most carts are lost at the address step; filling in the city from the PIN code could cut that.”
“Most carts are lost at the delivery-fee step; showing the fee on product pages could cut that.”
quiz.explanation: The drops are 70 at login, 80 at the address step, 90 at the delivery-fee step and 420 at payment. Payment loses more carts than the other three steps together, so the insight and its action belong there.
quiz.why_wrong: Guest checkout is the right action when most carts are lost at login, but only 70 of 1,000 are; filling in the city from the PIN code suits a funnel where the address form loses most carts, but here it loses 80; showing the fee early is right when the fee step loses most, but it loses 90, against 420 at payment.
quiz.learning_outcome: Tie the insight and its action to where the numbers show the biggest problem.

quiz.title: One season’s data
quiz.scenario: A school-bag brand asks how much stock to hold for next June’s school reopening. Your analysis of its website rests on two weeks of orders, all during this year’s reopening.
quiz.question: What should your memo say about the data?
options: Say the weeks may not be typical of the year, and that the numbers are only a rough guide
Hold the memo until a full year of data is in, since one season can’t support a plan
Base the plan on the two weeks, and note that they cover a single reopening season
Scale each week down by the usual reopening uplift, and plan from a normal month
quiz.explanation: The decision is about next June’s reopening, so two reopening weeks are the right evidence, not an unusual sample. The limit that matters is that they come from one season, so say that.
quiz.why_wrong: Warning that the weeks aren’t typical of the year would be right if the memo were about normal months, but it is about the next reopening, where these weeks are typical; waiting for a full year would suit a year-round decision with no deadline, but a year of normal months adds little to a reopening plan; scaling the weeks down to a normal month throws away exactly the reopening demand the plan needs.
quiz.learning_outcome: Whether data is typical depends on the decision it supports.

quiz.title: Did the loyalty programme pay?
quiz.scenario: Six months ago a café chain launched a loyalty programme in 9 of its 10 cities on the same day; the tenth, Shillong, is its only café in a tourist town. Members were already its biggest spenders before they joined, and sales grew in every city this year. The chain’s gross margin is 60%, and the programme has cost ₹15 lakh. The CFO asks whether it has paid for itself.
quiz.question: Which answer should you give?
options: “Yes: members spent ₹61 lakh more than all non-members over the six months, so ₹37 lakh of gross profit against ₹15 lakh of cost.”
“Yes: members spent ₹45 lakh more than in their six months before joining, so ₹27 lakh of gross profit against ₹15 lakh of cost.”
“Yes: members spent ₹38 lakh more than non-members who spent as much before, so ₹23 lakh of gross profit against ₹15 lakh of cost.”
“No: the nine cities grew only ₹20 lakh more than Shillong, which has no programme, so ₹12 lakh of gross profit against ₹15 lakh of cost.”
quiz.explanation: Non-members who spent as much before the programme are a fair comparison for members, who were already big spenders. Their ₹38 lakh of extra spend at a 60% margin is about ₹23 lakh of gross profit, so after the ₹15 lakh cost the programme has made about ₹8 lakh.
quiz.why_wrong: All non-members would be a fair comparison if members had been typical customers, but they were already the biggest spenders, so ₹61 lakh overstates the effect; before and after would work if sales were otherwise flat, but they grew in every city, so some of the ₹45 lakh would have come anyway; a city without the programme is a good comparison when cities are alike, but Shillong is the chain’s only tourist town, so its sales follow different visitors.
quiz.learning_outcome: Net impact = extra gross profit against a fair comparison, minus the cost.

questions.title: Is our marketing working?
questions.scenario: The founder of a Kochi skincare brand spent ₹12 lakh on Instagram and Google ads in Q2 (April to June), and asks you, “Is our marketing working?”
questions.question: Which version of the question can your analysis actually answer, and use?
options: “Did Instagram or Google bring Q2 first orders at a lower cost each, and should budget move?”
“How did Instagram and Google do in Q2, judging by the likes, clicks and reach each one got?”
“Which channel brought the most new customers in Q2, Instagram or Google?”
“Did revenue rise in the Q2 months when we spent more on marketing?”
questions.explanation: It names the channels, the period, a measure that links spend to customers (cost per first order) and the decision it informs (whether to move budget).
questions.why_wrong: Likes, clicks and reach measure attention, not whether the spend brought customers; the most new customers ignores how much each channel cost, so it can’t say where the next rupee should go; revenue rising in high-spend months is timing, not proof that marketing caused it.
questions.learning_outcome: A question becomes answerable when it names a measure, a period and a decision.

questions.title: The red stores
questions.scenario: A pharmacy chain’s dashboard turns a store red on any day its sales are below ₹45,000, so managers can check the next morning for a stock-out or a closed counter. Its stores differ up to three-fold in size. Store 12 takes ₹38,000–42,000 every Tuesday and ₹46,000–52,000 on other days, so it turns red every Tuesday, and managers now ignore the colour.
questions.question: Which change would make the red flag most useful?
options: Flag a store on a day its sales fall below its own range for that weekday
Flag a store when its 7-day average sales fall below its own usual range
Keep the ₹45,000 line, but turn a store red only after two low days in a row
Set one lower line of ₹35,000 for every store, so red appears much less often
questions.explanation: Store 12’s Tuesdays are always low, so a Tuesday should be compared with its own usual Tuesdays. Each store’s range for each weekday keeps the flag to real problems, and still flags a bad day by the next morning, which is what managers need.
questions.why_wrong: A 7-day average against the store’s range is right for spotting a lasting decline, but it moves slowly, so one bad day, such as a closed counter, never shows the next morning; two low days in a row would cut false alarms if low days were scattered at random, but one line can’t suit stores three-fold apart in size, and a one-day problem is missed; one lower line for all would suit a chain-wide minimum, such as covering rent, but a big store could lose half its sales before turning red.
questions.learning_outcome: Set alerts against each measure’s own normal variation, at the speed the decision needs.

questions.title: The SKUs that won’t match
questions.scenario: A wholesaler in Nagpur uses =XLOOKUP(B2, Master[SKU], Master[Category], "New SKU"). It shows “New SKU” on 300 of 4,000 invoice lines, but when you search the master by eye, those SKUs are there.
questions.question: What is the most likely cause?
options: The master isn’t sorted A to Z, and XLOOKUP needs sorted data to find an exact match
Some SKUs differ by hidden spaces, or are text in one sheet and numbers in the other
XLOOKUP is doing an approximate match, because the fourth argument wasn’t set to exact
The Category cells are blank for those SKUs, so XLOOKUP shows the not-found text
questions.explanation: A lookup matches only identical values. A trailing space, or a SKU stored as text in one sheet and as a number in the other, looks the same on screen but doesn’t match. Clean and convert both columns, then look up again.
questions.why_wrong: XLOOKUP’s default exact match doesn’t need sorted data; the fourth argument is the not-found value, and the default match is already exact; a found SKU with a blank category returns a blank (shown as 0), not the not-found text.
questions.learning_outcome: When a lookup fails on values that look equal, check spaces and data types.

questions.title: The AI’s cleaning step
questions.scenario: A coaching centre in Kota has 9,400 enquiry rows (student_name, phone, course, enquiry_date). Brothers and sisters often share one phone, a student may enquire about two courses, and the centre counts one enquiry per student per course. An AI assistant suggests df = df.drop_duplicates(subset="student_name"), which leaves 7,100 rows.
questions.question: Which line should replace the assistant’s?
options: df = df.drop_duplicates(subset=["student_name", "phone", "course"])
df = df.drop_duplicates(subset=["student_name", "phone"], keep="first")
df = df.drop_duplicates(subset=["phone", "course"], keep="first")
df = df.drop_duplicates(keep="first", ignore_index=True)
questions.explanation: The centre counts one enquiry per student per course, and a student is best told apart by name and phone together, since siblings share a phone. So a repeat enquiry is the same name, phone and course; anything else is a different student or a different course.
questions.why_wrong: Name and phone would be right if each student enquired about one course only, but it merges one student’s two courses into one; phone and course would be right if each phone belonged to one student, but it merges brothers and sisters who enquire about the same course; with no subset only rows identical in every column go, which would catch exact export copies, but repeat enquiries have different dates, so they stay.
questions.learning_outcome: Choose the columns that define a duplicate from what one record means to the business.

questions.title: The blank incomes
questions.scenario: An NGO in Bhopal surveyed 2,000 households on tablets about monthly income, for a funding report. The income question was on a screen that failed to load for a random 30% of households, so 600 have no answer. Every household that saw the question answered it. The report is due to the funder next week.
questions.question: What should the report give for average income?
options: No average yet: re-survey the 600 households first, so the figure covers all 2,000
The average with each of the 600 blanks filled with the median of the 1,400 answers
The average of the 1,400 answers, noting that 600 were missed at random by a screen fault
The average of the 1,400 answers, with the margin of error for a sample of 1,400
questions.explanation: The screen failed at random, so the 1,400 who answered are a random mix of the 2,000 and their average stands for everyone; leaving out a random mix changes little. Report the share missing and why, so readers know the gap isn’t a bias.
questions.why_wrong: Re-surveying the 600 would be right if the gap were not random, for example if the screen failed only on the tablets used in rural blocks, but a random fault leaves 1,400 answers that stand for all 2,000, and the report is due next week; filling 600 blanks with the median invents incomes and makes the result look more certain than it is; a margin of error is worth adding if the funder asks how precise the figure is, but alone it doesn’t say that 600 households are missing or why.
questions.learning_outcome: Why data is missing decides what to report: a random gap needs stating, not correcting.

questions.title: Big payments by method
questions.scenario: A fintech app’s payments table has one row per payment (payment_id, method, amount). An analyst runs: SELECT method, COUNT(*) FROM payments WHERE amount > 1000 GROUP BY method;
questions.question: What does the query return?
options: The total amount paid above ₹1,000, for each payment method
The payment methods that have more than 1,000 payments
The average payment for each method, for payments over ₹1,000
The number of payments above ₹1,000 for each method
questions.explanation: WHERE keeps payments above ₹1,000; GROUP BY method with COUNT(*) counts them per method.
questions.why_wrong: COUNT(*) counts payments, it doesn’t add amounts; the 1,000 filters each payment’s amount, not the number of payments; COUNT isn’t AVG.
questions.learning_outcome: Read WHERE as a row filter and COUNT(*) as a count per group.

questions.title: Customers and their orders
questions.scenario: An online bookshop’s customers table has 5,000 rows, and 3,200 of those customers have ordered. Its orders table has 9,000 rows, each with a customer_id that is in customers.
questions.question: How many rows does customers INNER JOIN orders ON customer_id return, and who is left out?
options: 10,800 rows: every order, plus one row for each customer who never ordered
3,200 rows, one per customer who ordered, with repeat orders folded into one
9,000 rows, one per order; the 1,800 customers who never ordered are left out
5,000 rows, one per customer, with blank order columns for those who never ordered
questions.explanation: An inner join keeps only rows that match in both tables, once per match. Every order matches one customer, so there are 9,000 rows, and the 5,000 − 3,200 = 1,800 customers with no order have no match and drop out.
questions.why_wrong: Every order plus the never-ordered customers is a LEFT JOIN from customers, which keeps customers with no match; one row per ordering customer would need a GROUP BY, while a join repeats a customer once per order; one row per customer with blanks is neither join: a left join keeps blanks but still repeats customers once per order.
questions.learning_outcome: An inner join keeps only matching rows, once per match: count rows from the matches.

questions.title: Month-on-month change
questions.scenario: A monthly revenue table starts in January 2026. A query adds revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS change.
questions.question: What does the change column show?
options: Each month’s change from the month before; January’s is NULL, as it has no earlier row
Each month’s change from the month before; January’s equals its revenue, as the gap counts as 0
Each month’s change from the month after; December’s is NULL, as it has no later row
Each month’s change from January, the first month, so January’s change is 0
questions.explanation: LAG(revenue) puts the previous row’s revenue beside each month, in the order given. January has no earlier row, so LAG gives NULL, and revenue minus NULL is NULL.
questions.why_wrong: A missing value isn’t 0: arithmetic with NULL gives NULL, so January’s change is NULL, not its revenue; looking forward one row is LEAD, not LAG; LAG looks back one row each time, not always to the first month.
questions.learning_outcome: Use LAG for the previous period, and expect NULL where there is none.

questions.title: Household spending
questions.scenario: A survey of 1,500 households in Lucknow reports median monthly spending of ₹18,000 and a mean of ₹31,000.
questions.question: What does this suggest about the spending?
options: A few very low spenders pull the median down below what is typical
The data must contain errors, since the median and mean should be close
Most households spend more than ₹31,000, and a few spend very little
A few very high spenders pull the mean up: the data is skewed to the right
questions.explanation: When the mean is far above the median, a small number of very large values is pulling the mean up; half the households spend ₹18,000 or less.
questions.why_wrong: The median is the middle value, so a few low spenders can’t drag it down much, and low values would pull the mean below the median, not above it; a gap between mean and median is normal in skewed data like spending, not a sign of errors; if most spent more than ₹31,000, the median would be above ₹31,000.
questions.learning_outcome: A mean well above the median signals a few very large values.

questions.title: The new search page
questions.scenario: A travel-booking site’s A/B test of a new search page has run its planned 21 days. Version A converted 4.0% of 50,000 visitors and version B 4.1% of 50,000, a gap well within chance. B costs ₹1.5 lakh a month more to run.
questions.question: What should you recommend?
options: Run the test three more weeks, to see whether B’s small lead becomes significant
Launch B: it converted more visitors than A over the test’s full planned length
Keep A: the finished test shows no clear gain that would justify B’s extra cost
Launch B: the test shows it does no harm, and it is the newer, cleaner design
questions.explanation: The test ran its planned length, and 4.0% against 4.1% of 50,000 (about 2,000 against 2,050 sales) is within chance. With no clear difference, decide on other grounds: B costs ₹1.5 lakh a month more, so keep A.
questions.why_wrong: Running on would be right if the test had stopped before its planned length, but extending a finished test until a gap appears is the peeking mistake; launching B because it is ahead would be right if the gap were significant, but this one is within chance; launching B as no worse would be fair if B cost the same or less, but it costs ₹1.5 lakh a month more for no clear gain.
questions.learning_outcome: When a finished test shows no clear difference, decide on cost or simplicity, not on the tiny gap.

questions.title: The checkout test, city by city
questions.scenario: A D2C brand tested a new checkout for its planned 3 weeks, with 120,000 visitors in each group. Conversion rose from 3.0% to 3.6%, far beyond normal variation. In Tier-3 cities alone (3,000 visitors per group), conversion fell from 2.8% to 2.5%.
questions.question: What should your memo recommend?
options: Roll it out only in metro and Tier-2 cities, since Tier-3 conversion fell from 2.8% to 2.5%
Roll it out everywhere, watching Tier-3, since overall conversion rose from 3.0% to 3.6%
Hold the roll-out everywhere until Tier-3 cities, at 3,000 visitors a group, also show a rise
Roll it out everywhere, and report the 20% rise in conversion for every city, Tier-3 included
questions.explanation: Across 120,000 visitors a group, 3.0% to 3.6% is far beyond chance, and the test ran its planned length. In Tier-3 cities the fall is 84 against 75 sales out of 3,000 each, well within chance, so roll out and keep watching there.
questions.why_wrong: A metro and Tier-2 roll-out would be right if the Tier-3 fall were clear, for example the same fall with 30,000 visitors a group, but 9 sales out of 3,000 a group can’t show the design fails there; holding everyone back gives up a clear, tested gain because of a result that may be chance; the 20% rise is for all visitors together, and Tier-3 cities didn’t show it.
questions.learning_outcome: Act on the overall result, and treat a small subgroup’s result as uncertain.

questions.title: Revenue after the merge
questions.scenario: orders has 10,000 rows, one per order, with order_total, adding up to ₹82 lakh. After df = orders.merge(items, on="order_id"), where items(order_id, product, item_value) lists each product in an order, df has 26,000 rows and df["order_total"].sum() is ₹2.1 crore.
questions.question: What is the right way to get total revenue?
options: Run df.drop_duplicates() on the merged table, then sum order_total again
Redo the merge with how="left", so each order appears only once, then sum
Sum order_total in orders before the merge, or sum the item values after it
Divide ₹2.1 crore by the average number of items per order in the data
questions.explanation: Each order matches several items, so its order_total is repeated once per item. Summing at the order level before the merge, or summing item-level values after it, counts each rupee once.
questions.why_wrong: The merged rows differ in their item columns, so drop_duplicates() removes nothing; a left merge keeps orders without items but still repeats each order once per item; dividing by an average only approximates, because orders with many items are counted more than the average allows.
questions.learning_outcome: After a one-to-many merge, sum at the level where each value appears once.

questions.title: Nine brands
questions.scenario: A market report compares the share of sales of 9 instant-noodle brands across Indian cities.
questions.question: Which chart is clearest for comparing the brands?
options: A pie chart with all 9 slices, each one labelled with its share
A horizontal bar chart, sorted from largest share to smallest
A 100% stacked bar with all nine brands in a single bar
A donut chart sorted by share, with each slice labelled
questions.explanation: Sorted bars are read by length on a shared baseline, so nine brands are easy to compare and rank.
questions.why_wrong: Nine pie slices are hard to compare by angle, labels or not; in one stacked bar only the first segment starts at a shared baseline, so the rest are hard to compare; a donut has the same angle problem as a pie, and sorting doesn’t fix it.
questions.learning_outcome: Use a sorted bar chart to compare many categories.

questions.title: The 12% churn
questions.scenario: An AI assistant says your meditation app’s churn for March was 12%, and shows its working: March’s 1,200 cancellations divided by the 10,000 subscribers at the end of March. Your board defines churn as a month’s cancellations divided by the subscribers at the start of that month, which was 11,000. The figure is going into a board update.
questions.question: What should you do?
options: Use 12%: the working is shown, and 1,200 divided by 10,000 is correct arithmetic
Recompute it on the 11,000 subscribers at the start of March, about 10.9%
Use 12% if it sits inside the usual monthly churn range for subscription apps
Ask a second AI tool the same question, and use the figure if the two agree
questions.explanation: The assistant’s arithmetic is right, but it used end-of-month subscribers, and the board’s churn uses the start of the month. 1,200 ÷ 11,000 is about 10.9%, so recompute it on the board’s definition and say which definition you used.
questions.why_wrong: Shown working would be enough if its definition matched the board’s, but it divides by the wrong month-end base; the usual range catches a slip such as a misplaced decimal, but 12% and 10.9% both look normal, so it can’t tell them apart; a second tool may use a third definition, and two tools agreeing is a second opinion, not a check against the board’s rule.
questions.learning_outcome: Check an AI’s working against the definition your audience uses, then recompute.

questions.title: The memo’s first line
questions.scenario: 8 of a Tamil Nadu clinic chain’s 30 clinics, chosen at random, ran a 6-week test across 4,200 appointments: patients picked at random got an SMS reminder the day before. 11% of patients who got a reminder missed their appointment, against 18% of those who didn’t. An AI assistant drafted four opening lines for your memo to the operations head.
questions.question: Which opening line should you use?
options: “Recommendation: test day-before SMS reminders in more clinics first, since 8 of our 30 clinics may not stand for the whole chain.”
“Day-before SMS reminders end missed appointments, as our randomised test across the whole clinic chain has clearly proved.”
“Recommendation: send day-before SMS reminders in all 30 clinics; in an 8-clinic random test, 11% missed with one, 18% without.”
“We ran a 6-week randomised test of SMS reminders in 8 of our 30 clinics, covering 4,200 appointments; the method is set out below.”
questions.explanation: It leads with a decision the reader can act on and the number behind it, and it states the evidence exactly: patients with and without a reminder, compared at the same time in a random test. Randomly chosen clinics and patients make that strong enough to act on, and the roll-out can still be watched.
questions.why_wrong: The 8 clinics were chosen at random and the gap is large and clear, so another round of testing delays a cheap, proven gain; “end” and “the whole clinic chain” overstate a test that left 11% still missing in 8 clinics; opening with the method makes the reader hunt for the answer.
questions.learning_outcome: Lead with the action and state the evidence exactly, neither more nor less than it shows.

project.brief: Analyse 12 months of data for a real or realistic Indian business (for example a D2C brand, a café chain, a clinic or a coaching centre) and recommend one change that would grow revenue or cut costs. Your mentor helps you choose the business, the question and a dataset (a public dataset, or anonymised data a business shares with you).
deliverables: A one-page problem statement: the decision, who makes it, and how success will be measured
The cleaned dataset, with a short data dictionary and a cleaning log
Your SQL queries or Python notebook, with comments explaining each step, and a note of where an AI assistant helped and how you checked its work
A one-page dashboard (Power BI, Excel or Looker Studio) built around the decision
A one-page recommendation memo, and a 3-minute recorded walkthrough

rubric.name: Problem framing
rubric.description: One decision, who makes it, how success is measured, and the period, agreed with the mentor

rubric.name: Data quality
rubric.description: Raw file kept; every cleaning step logged with rows affected; gaps in the data stated

rubric.name: Analysis
rubric.description: Correct SQL or Python, joins checked, a key number reproduced; AI help disclosed and checked

rubric.name: Dashboard
rubric.description: Built around the decision: key numbers against target, honest axes, readable at a glance

rubric.name: Recommendation
rubric.description: Leads with the decision and its ₹ impact, states its limits, and the learner can explain every step
